candidateRows: The universe began to exist and therefore has a transcendent, personal cause beyond space and time.
This cosmological argument is the first of Craig's five principal reasons and directly supports the existence of supernatural agency.
Craig combines philosophical objections to an actual infinite past with cosmological evidence for a beginning, then characterizes the cause as a transcendent personal mind.
The universe's life-permitting fine-tuning is best explained by supernatural design rather than necessity or chance.
Fine-tuning is presented as a distinct principal argument in Craig's cumulative case and directly infers a supernatural designer.
Craig eliminates physical necessity, argues that chance and multiverse explanations are improbable or unsupported, and concludes that design explains fine-tuning.
Objective moral values exist, cannot be grounded by naturalism, and therefore are plausibly grounded in God.
The moral argument is one of the five expressly enumerated pillars of Craig's cumulative case for God's existence.
Craig contrasts moral experience with naturalistic relativism, argues that genuine moral obligations require supernatural grounding, and states a deductive conclusion to God.
The empty tomb, postmortem appearances, and disciples' belief are best explained by God's raising Jesus from the dead.
The resurrection case is a separately enumerated major argument intended to establish the existence of the God revealed by Jesus.
Craig identifies three claimed historical facts, rejects familiar naturalistic alternatives, and argues that resurrection is their best explanation and entails God's existence.
Immediate religious experience can provide a person with rational, direct knowledge that God exists.
Personal experience is Craig's fifth independent route to God's existence and completes the cumulative structure of his opening case.
Craig maintains that God may be known as an experienced reality and that attention to immediate experience supplies an avenue to theistic knowledge.
Naturalism is more reasonable because established natural knowledge deserves confidence while untestable supernatural bridges lack evidential support.
This passage supplies Shook's overarching epistemic case for naturalism and his governing standard for rejecting every supernatural inference in the debate.
Craig's cumulative claim that multiple arguments provide reliable bridges from natural evidence to supernatural reality.
Shook defines naturalism, places the burden on proposed theological bridges, argues that evidence-proof hypotheses gain no support, and favors continued natural inquiry.
Craig's cosmological inference does not establish God because timeless personhood is problematic and natural cosmological alternatives remain available.
This is Shook's principal response to Craig's first major argument, challenging both the proposed divine cause and the exclusion of natural alternatives.
Craig's argument that a finite cosmic beginning requires a timeless, spaceless, immaterial, and personal supernatural cause.
Shook questions the coherence of a timeless personal creator, disputes inferences from mathematical infinity, proposes further natural reality, and favors conservative suspension of belief.
Fine-tuning does not support divine design because the universe is hostile to life and adaptable theology is insulated from contrary evidence.
The passage directly contests Craig's second major argument by denying that observed cosmic conditions discriminate in favor of intentional design.
Craig's claim that the universe is extraordinarily fine-tuned for intelligent life and therefore points to a supernatural designer.
Shook distinguishes evolutionary adaptation from cosmic design, points to natural imperfection and hostility, and argues that theology accommodates either favorable or unfavorable observations.
Human-relative objective morality is possible without absolute supernatural truths, so Craig's moral definition begs the question.
This distinction between objective and absolute values is Shook's principal answer to a separately enumerated pillar of Craig's theistic case.
Craig's contention that objective moral values must be independent of humanity and therefore require grounding in supernatural reality.
Shook argues that Craig defines morality as transcendent at the outset, then defends revisable and human-relative objective truths without accepting absolute moral truths.
Shook's inability to establish that physical reality is all that exists leaves naturalism unsupported and internally incoherent.
This rebuttal challenges the foundation of the con position itself, arguing that criticism of theistic proofs cannot establish naturalism or atheism.
Shook's burden-of-proof framework under which naturalism remains reasonable without proving supernaturalism false or proving naturalism conclusively true.
Craig argues that naturalism affirms more than failed theistic proofs can establish, distinguishes atheism from agnosticism, and claims Shook cannot justify naturalism by his accepted methods.
Naturalism reasonably retains belief in nature while rejecting supernatural hypotheses that lack an evidential bridge.
This states Shook's core positive formulation of naturalism and directly addresses whether the available evidence warrants belief beyond nature.
Craig's contention that Shook had supplied no positive argument establishing philosophical naturalism.
Shook restates naturalism as belief that nature exists combined with rejection of supernatural bridges as unreasonable, then challenges inference from their unfalsifiability.
Fine-tuning does not establish design because other forms of life may be possible and the relevant probability space remains unknown.
The move contests a principal theistic argument by challenging both its life-centered assumption and its claimed probabilistic inference to a creator.
Craig's argument that the universe's life-permitting fine-tuning is best explained by intelligent design.

Shook argues that unfamiliar life might flourish under different physical conditions, that a creator's preference for humanlike life needs support, and that current ignorance defeats probability claims.
Objective morality can be sustained through humanity's collective moral and democratic practices without a supernatural lawgiver.
This supplies the naturalist's affirmative account of moral objectivity and directly challenges a major premise offered as evidence for God's existence.
Craig's claim that objective moral values and duties require a transcendent divine foundation.
Shook cites religious disagreement, democratic law, collective human wisdom, and humanist moral progress to argue that morality can remain objective without being absolute or divinely commanded.
The resurrection case lacks adequate independent historical corroboration and admits ordinary natural alternatives to the empty-tomb narrative.
The move attacks the historical reliability and explanatory force of Craig's principal specifically Christian argument for divine action.
Craig's appeal to Gospel-derived historical facts and the resurrection as their best explanation.

Shook disputes Craig's characterization of historical scholarship, objects to circular reliance on biblical materials, requests independent sources, and proposes natural complications for the tomb account.
God is needed to ground objective morality, not to give people knowledge of particular moral truths.
The distinction repairs the central moral argument by separating moral knowledge from moral ontology and preserving the claimed need for a transcendent standard.
Shook's objection that religious disagreement and moral change undermine religion's claim to objective moral truth.
Craig distinguishes epistemology from ontology, accepts instinctive moral knowledge and genuine moral progress, but argues that evolutionary products alone cannot supply an objective standard.
New Testament documents can function as historical sources without prior external corroboration when standard authenticity criteria support them.
This defends the evidential basis of the resurrection argument against the charge that Christian documents are inherently circular or historically unusable.
Shook's demand for non-Christian contemporary sources corroborating claims made in New Testament documents.
Craig mentions extra-biblical source surveys but principally rejects mandatory outside corroboration, invoking multiple attestation, embarrassment, dissimilarity, and related historical criteria.
The universe's beginning entails a transcendent cause and therefore falsifies the claim that nature is all that exists.
The move presents the cosmological argument's conclusion as direct evidence for a reality beyond the natural universe and against naturalism.
Shook's challenges to the Big Bang argument and his refusal to infer supernatural reality from current cosmology.
Craig says the causal premise and philosophical beginning argument remain intact, invokes contemporary cosmological testimony, and infers a transcendent cause beyond the universe.
Life-permitting fine-tuning excludes generic alternative life and supports intelligent design over physical necessity or chance.
The move consolidates the design argument by answering Shook's principal alternative-life objection and renewing the inference to an intelligent cosmic designer.
Shook's claims that different forms of life might exist and that multiverse possibilities weaken the fine-tuning inference.
Craig argues that altered constants would prevent stars, chemistry, matter, and complex self-replication altogether, so the observed fine-tuning still demands an explanation.
Naturalistic evolution cannot ground objective moral distinctions or genuine moral progress, whereas God can provide the required standard.
The move restates the moral argument as affirmative evidence for God by contrasting objective obligation with evolved social behavior and relativism.
Shook's humanist account of objective morality as collective wisdom independent of a divine foundation.
Craig distinguishes grounding from moral discernment, characterizes evolved values as programmed and non-objective, and argues that real wrongdoing and progress imply God.
Fine-tuning should not prompt a design inference because scientific expansion of the relevant cosmic population can dissolve apparent uniqueness.
The move gives Shook's closing answer to the design argument by connecting past discoveries of many planets with prospective discoveries of broader cosmic domains.
Craig's closing claim that cosmic fine-tuning demands explanation by an intelligent designer rather than natural alternatives.
Shook analogizes the once-special Earth to the observed diversity of planets, extends the pattern to universes, and urges confidence that scientific inquiry may naturalize apparent fine-tuning.
The historical record of Jesus's claims, miracles, and resurrection is best explained by his divine identity and God's raising him from the dead.
This restates the debate's historical case for specifically Christian theism and explains why the evidence is claimed to identify God with Jesus's revelation.
The question asks why evidence for a generic God should establish the God revealed in the Bible.
During audience questioning, Craig returns to his historical argument and presents the resurrection as divine confirmation of Jesus's exceptional claims.
Miracle testimony does not establish supernatural causation because testimony requires corroboration and many alleged wonders have plausible natural explanations.
The move directly challenges experiential evidence for supernaturalism by offering a general evidential standard and a naturalistic treatment of miracle reports.
The audience question asks how atheism explains reported modern miracles such as healings and Fatima.
Shook compares miracle reports with other extraordinary testimony, invokes corroboration and scientific alternatives, and notes inconsistent treatment of rival religions' claims.
Nonexistence can sometimes be proved, and failure to disprove God would not justify naturalism's categorical denial of supernatural reality.
The move contests a stated burden-of-proof principle and argues that strong naturalistic conclusions exceed what their defender claims can be demonstrated.
The questioner asserts that one cannot prove a thing's nonexistence while objecting to God as an explanation.
Craig supplies ordinary and logical examples of demonstrated nonexistence, then argues that an inability to disprove God should produce agnosticism rather than naturalism.
Craig's theistic arguments are deductive rather than explanatory hypotheses, so their force depends on the premises' plausibility and necessary implication.
The distinction specifies how Craig's principal arguments are meant to support the motion and rejects a criticism aimed at inference to the best explanation.
The questioner argues that invoking an inherently inexplicable God adds a problem instead of advancing knowledge.
Craig says the objection misclassifies his case: if the stated premises are more plausible than their denials, the theistic conclusion follows deductively.
Naturalism is a conservative conclusion from nature's known existence plus the failure of purported bridges from nature to supernatural reality.
This states the core architecture of Shook's case: affirm the observed natural world and withhold supernatural belief when supporting arguments fail.
The question challenges whether naturalism can be treated as the default when only this universe is directly known.
Shook distinguishes the premise that nature exists from the conclusion that only nature is reasonably believable, grounding the latter in failed supernatural arguments.
Moral experience presents objective obligations and values as real, contradicting naturalism and supplying the moral argument's premise for God's existence.
The move defends a principal argument for the motion by treating moral experience as evidence against naturalism and for a deductive theistic conclusion.
The questioner asks why humans must be special and morality objective rather than merely a preferred conclusion.
Craig argues that people cannot consistently live as moral nihilists and that naturalists should take moral experience seriously alongside reason and science.
When supernatural claims lack adequate justification, atheism and agnosticism share the same rational default of withholding belief in supernatural existence.
The move defends atheistic nonbelief against the charge that evidential conservatism requires agnosticism and clarifies the epistemic posture of the con side.
The audience member argues that admitting evidential uncertainty should lead to the more conservative agnostic position.
Shook grants logical possibilities but maintains that unsupported possibilities do not merit belief, leaving little substantive difference between atheism and agnosticism.
Conflicting religious experiences cannot reliably establish supernatural truth because rival claimants cannot all be correct and no sound method selects among them.
The argument directly undercuts experiential evidence for God by claiming that pervasive incompatibility prevents such experiences from identifying supernatural reality.
The audience member asks why religious experience is disregarded as valid support for the existence of God.
Shook surveys incompatible reports of gods and revelations, including divisions within Christianity, and concludes that the experiences warrant study but not supernatural inference.
Moral experience is properly treated as basically reliable, like sense experience, unless there is a positive reason to regard it as delusory.
This provides the epistemological defense of the moral premise in Craig's theistic argument and connects objective moral differences to God's necessary existence.
The moderator asks Craig to defend the premise that humans are special and objective moral values exist.
Craig argues that neither sensory nor moral experience can be validated from wholly outside itself, so both remain warranted absent a defeater.
Shared comparison of fallible moral perspectives can yield objective but nonabsolute morality, while moral confusion and change count against divine implantation.
The move supplies a naturalistic account of moral knowledge and turns the character of moral experience into counterevidence against a transcendent moral source.
The moderator asks where moral experience comes from if it has no divine or supernatural cause.
Shook characterizes moral life as difficult and internally mixed, arguing that intersubjective deliberation creates progress more plausibly than revelation does.
